newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-French economy's weak 97 start bodes ill.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-French economy's weak 97 start bodes ill.

text.p: The French economy got off to a weak start in the first three months of 1997 and economists said it was a bad omen for growth in the rest of a year which is the one that counts in qualifying for European monetary union.

French national statistics institute INSEE said the economy grew by 0.2 percent in the first three months of the year, lower than a 0.4 percent increase predicted by economists, and the same rate as the last quarter of 1996.

The outgoing centre-right government had hoped investment and stock rebuilding would be an engine of growth this year, but economists said marked declines in both components demonstrated a worrying lack of confidence among French businesses.

Joanne Perez, strategist at Merrill Lynch, said even though consumer demand had picked up companies were being dissuaded from embarking on new investment or replenishing inventories because prices were either stable or edging down.

"All of those (factors) suggest companies are very concerned about margins, about orders. I can't see a major...new dynamic force until the fourth quarter. I honestly don't see anything in the figures to think growth will exceed two percent this year, Perez said.

The centre-right coalition just ousted from power forecast a minimum growth rate in 1997 of 2.3 percent, including a prediction that investment would rise three percent and stock rebuilding would add 0.3 percentage points to the growth rate.

"The figures are not as good as we expected. They confirm that the internal motor has not started," Emmanuel Ferry, economist at Credit Commercial de France said. "The weakest component was company investment, which is worrying as it is a factor blocking the recovery."

One factor contributing to lower than expected growth was that there were fewer working days than in the last three months of 1996 which Philippe Brossard, head of research, at ABN Amro Finance said could be a reason for the decline in stock levels.
INSEE said the lower number of working days had knocked 0.25 percentage points off growth and some economists said once this was taken into account the growth outlook was positive.

"It's pretty much in line with our expectations. In our view it was the final quarter of a slow recovery trend which started in 1996. From here on we expect a strong acceleration in the second quarter and in the second half," David Naude, economist at JP Morgan. "It's partly affected by the negative working days impact."

The new Socialist government, elected by discontented voters on a mandate to boost growth and reduce record 12.8 percent unemployment, will also be hoping for a quick turnaround in the French economy.
"The window of opportunity (for the Socialists) is quite short. They will be judged on employment record with amazing rapidity," Perez said.
